The American toad (Anaxyrus americanus) undergoes a complex life cycle that begins with a gelatinous egg mass deposited in shallow freshwater ponds. Each individual egg is initially quite small, and upon hatching, the free-swimming tadpole emerges at a wet weight of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. At a constant water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time from oviposition to hatching is approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], a developmental rate consistent with those reported for other bufonids breeding in cool, ephemeral wetlands. Following eclosion, the endotrophic larva relies entirely on its residual yolk reserves before transitioning to active filter feeding. This brief yolk-sac stage is a critical period of rapid organogenesis and early morphological differentiation, after which the tadpoles begin grazing on periphyton and suspended organic matter.

During the aquatic tadpole phase, larvae grow steadily, undergoing a dramatic morphological transformation at metamorphosis. After approximately 55 days  from hatching, maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the fully developed tadpole reaches metamorphic climax, characterized by tail resorption, limb bud development, and gill regression. The recently metamorphosed toadlet emerges at a snout-vent length (SVL) of about 1 centimeter  and a corresponding wet weight of 0.18 grams . This small size at the onset of the terrestrial phase makes these recruits vulnerable to desiccation and predation, though their cryptic coloration and noxious skin secretions offer some protection as they disperse into surrounding upland habitats.

Following the larval-juvenile transition, the terrestrial juvenile amphibian embarks on a period of sustained growth that continues for several years. Under controlled laboratory conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time from metamorphosis to the attainment of sexual maturity is about 3 years [tp = about 3 years]. At this point, individuals are typically around 9 centimeters [Lp = around 9 centimeters] in total length, a size that marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the ability to participate in breeding choruses. Growth trajectories differ markedly between the sexes, a pattern common among anurans, and this size at puberty represents a threshold beyond which energy is increasingly invested in reproductive rather than somatic tissues.

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in Anaxyrus americanus, with females consistently attaining larger ultimate body dimensions than males. Field surveys indicate that female toads reach a maximum SVL of 11.1 centimeters [Li = 11.1 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight of 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams], whereas the largest males rarely exceed 8.5 centimeters [Li = 8.5 centimeters] in SVL and weigh approximately 54 grams [Wwi = approximately 54 grams] at their asymptotic size. This disparity is thought to reflect the selective advantages of larger female body size for producing larger clutches, while males benefit from earlier maturation and smaller body size that facilitates mobility during chorus attendance.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, with gravid females depositing between 4,000 and 12,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 4,000 and 12,000 eggs per clutch] in a single breeding event each spring [F_R_i = single breeding event each spring] at an ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The maximum recorded longevity for wild individuals at 15 °C is approximately 36 years [am = approximately 36 years], an exceptionally long lifespan for a small-bodied anuran that underscores a slow life-history pace characterized by delayed maturity and high at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]adult survival. This combination of high fecundity and extended reproductive lifespan allows populations to buffer against periodic recruitment failures in variable pond environments.
